Required Packages:¶

  • NumPy: For arrays, and various linear algebra operations.
  • Matplotlib: For visualizing and viewing images.
  • Scikit Learn: For Olivetti faces dataset, PCA, LDA models and metrics.
  • Jupyter Lab: For running Jupyter Notebooks.

All these packages are mentioned in requirements.txt

In [1]:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import fetch_olivetti_faces, make_blobs
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display, Math

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA):¶

LDA is a supervised machine learning and statistical technique used for classification and dimensionality reduction. It projects data from high dimensions to lower dimensions, while maximising between class separation and minimising within-class scatter.

PCA projects onto lower dimensions while preserving maximum variance, however maximum variance does not guarantee maximum class separation. Also face recognition is a supervised learning problems because we have to deal with labeled dataset. However this does not leave behind PCA, instead PCA plays a key role in creating an effective LDA based model.

PCA-based face representation are commonly referred as Eigenfaces, while PCA followed by LDA produces Fisherfaces.

The mathematics:¶

Suppose a dataset has $n$ features, $N$ samples and $C$ classes.

For LDA, we have to maximize the distance between the means of classes, i.e. $S_{b}=\sum_{c=1}^{C}{N_{c}(\mu_c-\mu)(\mu_c-\mu)^{T}}$ and minimize the within class scatter, i.e. $S_w=\sum_{c=1}^{C}{\sum_{x\in c}{(x-\mu_c)(x-\mu_c)^{T}}}$

The objective function for LDA becomes: $$\begin{align} & J = \frac{w^{T}S_bw}{w^{T}S_ww} \implies S_{b}w=\lambda S_{w}w \end{align}$$ The vector $w$ gives the direction of maximum separability, and the $S_bw=\lambda S_ww$ is the generalized eigenvalue problem which can be solved computationally using scipy.linalg.eigh(S_b, S_w)

There are some additional constraints that we need to take care of:

  1. $S_b$ can only have atmost rank of $C-1$, which leads to atmost $C-1$ non-zero eigenvalues. Hence we can only reduce dimensions $\leq C-1$
  2. If $rank(S_w)\leq N-C$, till this condition it is non-singular. For $n>N-C$, $S_w$ becomes singular.

Solution for this:

To force invertability on $S_w$ we add a factor of $\gamma I$. Also we reduce the features i.e. the dimensions of the original dataset using PCA to solve the second constraint.

After finding the directions in which the conditions are met, we have to project our higher dimension points onto the lower dimension.

Every new point is again projected on this lower dimensional subspace and the distance from class is measured. Whichever class is near is the predicted class!

A from scratch implementation exists in this project. It can found at LDA/linear_discriminant_analysis.py

Visualizing LDA:¶

First we'll need to make a synthetic dataset and plot it.

In [2]:
X, y = make_blobs(
    n_samples=200,
    n_features=2,
    centers=2,
    random_state=42
)

X0, X1 = X[y == 0], X[y == 1]
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7.5))
plt.scatter(X0[:, 0], X0[:, 1], color="red", label="Class 0")
plt.scatter(X1[:, 0], X1[:, 1], color="green", label="Class 1")
plt.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.show()

Projecting data from higher dimensional space to lower dimensional sub-space:¶

We will use the from-scratch implementation here.

In [3]:
from LDA.linear_discriminant_analysis import LDA

lda = LDA(n_components=1)
projection = lda.fit_transform(X, y)
projection0, projection1 = projection[y == 0], projection[y == 1]

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 7.5))
plt.scatter(projection0.flatten(), [0]*len(projection0), color="red", label="Class 0")
plt.scatter(projection1.flatten(), [0]*len(projection1), color="green", label="Class 1")
plt.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.axhline(y=0)
plt.show()

Application to Face Recognition:¶

Here we will use the implementation from Scikit Learn. The logic is same, maximize the between class separability and minimize within class separability.

Perform PCA if needed.

Since, we are using Olivetti faces dataset, the dataset has 40 subjects with 10 images each and size 4096. The size becomes the features for the dataset.

For train-test split we will keep 8 images for each subject in the training dataset and remaining in the test dataset.

So there would be $8\times 40=320$ samples and $40$ classes and features must be $\leq 320-40\implies\leq280$

We will reduce this to our $4096$ features dataset to $80$ features and use $30$ components for LDA.

Dataset preparation:¶

First we will prepare our dataset. For that we need to setup some constants.

In [4]:
N_SUBJECTS = 40
TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT = 8
TEST_PER_SUBJECT = 2
IMG_SIZE = 4096
IMG_SHAPE = (64, 64)
TOTAL_IMAGES = 400
IMAGES_PER_SUBJECT = 10
PCA__N_COMPONENTS = 80
LDA__N_COMPONENTS = 30

Creating train test datasets:¶

As mentioned, train dataset will have 8 images of 40 subjects and test dataset will have 2 images of 40 subjects.

In [5]:
dataset = fetch_olivetti_faces()
images = dataset.data

train_dataset = np.empty((N_SUBJECTS, TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT, IMG_SIZE))
test_dataset = np.empty((N_SUBJECTS, TEST_PER_SUBJECT, IMG_SIZE))

for i in range(0, TOTAL_IMAGES, IMAGES_PER_SUBJECT):
    train_dataset[i//IMAGES_PER_SUBJECT, :, :] = images[i:i+TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT]
    test_dataset[i//IMAGES_PER_SUBJECT, :, :] = images[i+TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT:i+IMAGES_PER_SUBJECT]

train_dataset = train_dataset.reshape(-1, IMG_SIZE)
y_train = np.repeat(np.arange(N_SUBJECTS), TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT)
test_dataset = test_dataset.reshape(-1, IMG_SIZE)
y_test = np.repeat(np.arange(N_SUBJECTS), TEST_PER_SUBJECT)

Creating pipeline:¶

Now we need to create a pipeline which will first perform PCA to reduce features from 4096 to 150, and then perform LDA.

In [6]:
pca = PCA(n_components=PCA__N_COMPONENTS, random_state=42)
lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=LDA__N_COMPONENTS)

model = Pipeline([("pca", pca), ("lda", lda)])
model.fit(train_dataset, y_train)
Out[6]:

Parameters
n_components n_components: int, float or 'mle', default=None

Number of components to keep.
if n_components is not set all components are kept::

n_components == min(n_samples, n_features)

If ``n_components == 'mle'`` and ``svd_solver == 'full'``, Minka's
MLE is used to guess the dimension. Use of ``n_components == 'mle'``
will interpret ``svd_solver == 'auto'`` as ``svd_solver == 'full'``.

If ``0 < n_components < 1`` and ``svd_solver == 'full'``, select the
number of components such that the amount of variance that needs to be
explained is greater than the percentage specified by n_components.

If ``svd_solver == 'arpack'``, the number of components must be
strictly less than the minimum of n_features and n_samples.

Hence, the None case results in::

n_components == min(n_samples, n_features) - 1 		80
random_state random_state: int, RandomState instance or None, default=None

Used when the 'arpack' or 'randomized' solvers are used. Pass an int
for reproducible results across multiple function calls.
See :term:`Glossary <random_state>`.

.. versionadded:: 0.18.0 		42
copy copy: bool, default=True

If False, data passed to fit are overwritten and running
fit(X).transform(X) will not yield the expected results,
use fit_transform(X) instead. 		True
whiten whiten: bool, default=False

When True (False by default) the `components_` vectors are multiplied
by the square root of n_samples and then divided by the singular values
to ensure uncorrelated outputs with unit component-wise variances.

Whitening will remove some information from the transformed signal
(the relative variance scales of the components) but can sometime
improve the predictive accuracy of the downstream estimators by
making their data respect some hard-wired assumptions. 		False
svd_solver svd_solver: {'auto', 'full', 'covariance_eigh', 'arpack', 'randomized'}, default='auto'

"auto" :
The solver is selected by a default 'auto' policy is based on `X.shape` and
`n_components`: if the input data has fewer than 1000 features and
more than 10 times as many samples, then the "covariance_eigh"
solver is used. Otherwise, if the input data is larger than 500x500
and the number of components to extract is lower than 80% of the
smallest dimension of the data, then the more efficient
"randomized" method is selected. Otherwise the exact "full" SVD is
computed and optionally truncated afterwards.
"full" :
Run exact full SVD calling the standard LAPACK solver via
`scipy.linalg.svd` and select the components by postprocessing
"covariance_eigh" :
Precompute the covariance matrix (on centered data), run a
classical eigenvalue decomposition on the covariance matrix
typically using LAPACK and select the components by postprocessing.
This solver is very efficient for n_samples >> n_features and small
n_features. It is, however, not tractable otherwise for large
n_features (large memory footprint required to materialize the
covariance matrix). Also note that compared to the "full" solver,
this solver effectively doubles the condition number and is
therefore less numerical stable (e.g. on input data with a large
range of singular values).
"arpack" :
Run SVD truncated to `n_components` calling ARPACK solver via
`scipy.sparse.linalg.svds`. It requires strictly
`0 < n_components < min(X.shape)`
"randomized" :
Run randomized SVD by the method of Halko et al.

Fisherfaces:¶

Now we will take a look at first few fisherfaces.

In [7]:
fisherfaces = pca.components_.T @ lda.scalings_[:, :LDA__N_COMPONENTS]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(16, 13))

for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flatten()):
    ax.imshow(fisherfaces[:, i].reshape(IMG_SHAPE), cmap="gray")
    ax.set_title(f"Fisherface {i+1}")
    ax.axis("off")

plt.show()

These fisherfaces jointly capture discriminating facial regions; such as jaw edges and eye spacing, that reliably differ between individuals while staying stable within each person's own variations.

Testing the model:¶

We will now use the test_dataset to evaluate out model.

Picking a test image:¶

We will randomly select a test image.

In [8]:
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=144)
test_image_idx = rng.integers(0, TEST_PER_SUBJECT*N_SUBJECTS, size=1)
test_image_vector = test_dataset[test_image_idx]

Finding class of test face:¶

Now we will predict the class of the test face. This will only tell us the predicted class, but we will pick a random face from predicted class and compare them.

In [9]:
predicted_class = model.predict(test_image_vector)

random_img_idx = rng.integers(0, TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT, size=1)
predicted_class_subject = train_dataset[predicted_class*TRAIN_PER_SUBJECT+random_img_idx, :].reshape(IMG_SHAPE)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(16, 10))

axes[0].imshow(test_image_vector.reshape(IMG_SHAPE), cmap="gray", interpolation="bilinear")
axes[0].set_title("Test Image")

axes[1].imshow(predicted_class_subject, cmap="gray", interpolation="bilinear")
axes[1].set_title("Image from predicted class")

for ax in axes:
    ax.axis("off")

plt.show()

Some important metrics:¶

Since the test image is selected at random, there is a chance that the model did not show the failed case. Here we will take a look at Accuracy Score and Confusion Matrix.

Accuracy Score:¶

In [10]:
y_predicted = model.predict(test_dataset)

accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, y_predicted)*100
display(Math(r"\text{Accuracy Score}="+f"{accuracy}"+r"\%"))
$\displaystyle \text{Accuracy Score}=97.5\%$

The eigenfaces approach got us $88.8\%$ accuracy but our fisherfaces approach got us a $97.5\%$ accuracy! The dataset here used is small, so each misclassified image costs $1.25\%$ accuracy.

Confusion Matrix:¶

In [11]:
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_predicted)
figure, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(16, 10))
disp = ConfusionMatrixDisplay(confusion_matrix=cm)

disp.plot(ax=ax, cmap=plt.cm.Blues)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

This matrix tells us that for Subject 4 and 7, one image is classified correctly and other image is incorrectly classified.
